The Silicon Heartland Wants To Be America’s Next Chip Powerhouse

19

Shares

16

Intel may be the marquee name, but materials suppliers, packaging hubs, and quantum startups will determine whether the region becomes a true semiconductor ecosystem.

September 17th, 2026 -

By: Brendan Heffernan

Key Takeaways:

Major facility investments are driving momentum for the Midwestern semiconductor industry.
Workforce development remains a major structural challenge.
Quantum investment in Chicago represents a major opportunity for the regional semiconductor ecosystem.

The U.S. semiconductor industry has long been concentrated in established technology and manufacturing hubs, but new investments and startup activity are helping expand the industry’s footprint across the Midwest.
The prospect of a thriving Midwestern semiconductor industry has long hinged on whether semiconductor companies can leverage the region’s strong base of research institutions and available workforce, logistics, and industrial infrastructure to build a regional ecosystem. Over the last several years, that trend has gained momentum, with Intel and SK hynix bringing landmark facility investments to the Midwest, major bets on the future of quantum computing being made on the shores of Lake Michigan, and significant government investment being funneled toward semiconductor growth and startup support.
Defining the Midwestern ecosystem
The Midwest has undergone something of a “transformation” in recent years, with signs of a real semiconductor ecosystem beginning to materialize. “There’s always been this culture of innovation, but because a lot of the semiconductor and microelectronics work had existed on the coasts, or had been elsewhere, while the Midwest was really the heart for manufacturing, there’s been this transformation to a technology-based silicon heartland ecosystem,” said Matt Casto, CEO of Midwest Microelectronics Consortium (MMEC). “New foundry capabilities are being built just north of Columbus, Ohio. Supply chain manufacturers range from water treatment capabilities to semiconductor tools. We’ve got companies in the Midwest and in the state of Ohio now that are doing material growth development. So the building blocks for semiconductor work can connect within that Midwest ecosystem through additional supply chain capabilities. Now is a generational opportunity around advanced technology, and that requires a lot more emphasis on workforce development.”
The vision for this developing semiconductor ecosystem rests on a diverse technology production network that can integrate into the region’s existing manufacturing and research base. “One defining characteristic of the Midwest is its emphasis on connecting semiconductor innovation directly to manufacturing and industrial applications,” said Christopher Salomone, account management at Synopsys. “While some regions are heavily concentrated in either semiconductor design or fabrication, the Midwest is building a more integrated ecosystem that includes research institutions, advanced manufacturing, automotive technology, defense applications, and emerging semiconductor production capabilities.”
One of the biggest markers of the industry’s Midwestern development has been Intel’s $28B+ “Silicon Heartland” project in suburban Central Ohio. Expected to open in the early 2030s, the facility will create 3,000 new Intel jobs in the metro Columbus area once fully operational.
“Intel’s investment helped establish the Midwest as a serious contender in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and created opportunities that simply didn’t exist in this region before,” said Ted Geer, director of state government affairs for Ohio at Intel. “The Midwest has always produced exceptional engineers, researchers, and technical talent through its universities and research institutions. Too often, however, many of those graduates built their careers elsewhere. Today, students and researchers across the region can see a pathway to participate in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing without leaving the Midwest. Organizations like MMEC are helping build on that momentum by strengthening connections between research, talent development, and the future of domestic microelectronics.”
Part of the growing momentum also comes from established regional power players expanding their footprint with long-term growth in mind. “Brewer Science has been rooted in the Midwest since 1981, and our positioning isn’t incidental to the region; it’s strategic,” said Srikanth Kommu, co-CEO at Brewer Science. “We’ve demonstrated that world-class materials innovation and manufacturing can thrive outside traditional coastal hubs, which directly challenges the historical consolidation of semiconductor ecosystems. When you connect that kind of regional leadership to what we’re doing on the ground, like our acquisition of Heraeus Epurio’s semiconductor chemicals business, which brought a production facility in Dayton, Ohio, into our operations, you start to see a materials corridor forming across the Midwest that didn’t exist five years ago. Our deliberate geographic deepening through acquisitions and internal growth, from Rolla to Vichy to Springfield to now Dayton, treats our supply chain and workforce as strategic assets. This model lets us sustain margins while investing in facility upgrades, process improvements, and worker development. The manufacturers who will matter most in this region are those treating this as a 20-year investment in institutional capability, not a response to quarterly performance metrics.”

Still, long-standing workforce challenges remain a hurdle to the industry’s potential to reshape the regional economy.
Filling the gaps in workforce development and funding
While encouraging activities are underway, the Midwest’s industry identity isn’t completely defined yet. “Every successful technology cluster develops its own identity and strengths over time,” said Intel’s Geer. “The Midwest brings a unique combination of engineering talent, manufacturing expertise, practicality, and a culture that values collaboration and getting things done. As global demand for semiconductors continues to grow, we’ll have an opportunity to see how those Midwestern strengths shape the industry’s future. Semiconductors are foundational to artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and many of the technologies that power the modern economy. I believe the Midwest has real potential to become a leading center for semiconductor innovation and manufacturing.”
The two biggest obstacles to the Midwestern semiconductor industry becoming a reality are existing gaps in workforce development and sustainable capital funding. “Two challenges will determine whether this regional resurgence becomes durable: workforce velocity and capital market confidence. The Midwest needs to train and develop technicians, process engineers, and materials scientists faster than any regional initiative has previously managed,” Brewer Science’s Kommu said. “The gap between supply and demand will tighten significantly. This requires sustained investment in community college partnerships, apprenticeship programs, and industry-sponsored training, a 10-to-15-year commitment with uncertain ROI. On capital, public investment is substantial, but private capital deployment will determine sustainability. If private-sector growth follows the funding cycles of government initiatives, rather than organic market demand, the region risks boom-bust dynamics that damage competitiveness. We need self-sustaining business models that generate sufficient returns to reinvest, not ongoing subsidy dependence.”
Then, for the industry to scale regionally, the talent pool and capital support must grow alongside demand. “Talent development will be critical to sustaining long-term growth,” said Salomone. “Another important question is how effectively the industry can translate today’s public and private investments into a durable ecosystem that remains globally competitive over the next decade. Success will depend on continued collaboration between industry, academia, and government, as well as the ability to accelerate innovation while maintaining supply chain security and economic sustainability.”
These structural challenges are also driving creative strategies. “I don’t think we have all the answers, but I’d point to a few things we’ve done at Brewer Science that I believe are part of the answer,” Kommu said. “We became a Certified Employee-Owned company in 2020, which means the people doing the work also have a direct stake in the company’s success. That’s a meaningful lever for retention in a tight technical labor market. We’ve also chosen, deliberately, to grow by deepening our footprint in the Midwest rather than chasing the lowest-cost location every time. The companies that answer these workforce and capital questions well will be the ones that treat their people and their supply chain as long-term investments rather than variable costs. That’s the model we’re building here, and it’s a model other Midwest manufacturers can learn from.”
Quantum opportunities
The Midwest’s semiconductor industry may be well behind its coastal peers in many spheres of maturity, but there’s a concerted effort to avoid that fate when it comes to profiting from emerging quantum technologies. The Chicagoland region stands out as a hub for quantum investment, with $500 million in Illinois state funding for the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park and a planned $1 billion investment from PsiQuantum.
The University of Chicago-affiliated Chicago Quantum Exchange projects that emerging quantum technology could generate up to $80B in economic impact for Illinois, Wisconsin, and Indiana by 2035.
Quantum investment in the region is anchored by the planned Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park, which will house companies like IBM and PsiQuantum to conduct research on quantum applications for the pharmaceutical, chemistry, energy, defense, and other industries. The project will be built on part of the former U.S. Steel site on Chicago’s south side lakefront.
These investments put the Midwest in a globally competitive position. “The global economic trajectory for quantum information science and engineering has increased substantially and is expected to keep growing. If the Midwest keeps its foot on the pedal and continues launching initiatives 18 to 24 months ahead of others, the region can maintain its advantage,” said Kate Waimey Timmerman, CEO of the Chicago Quantum Exchange. “We have not often done that in other sectors. Many industries are already mature enough that it would be difficult for the Midwest to become a top two ecosystem, but quantum is still open. We are consistently listed among the leading U.S. quantum ecosystems. That said, this should not be viewed as a state-by-state competition. Quantum technology is a global undertaking, and there should be more collaboration across regions.”
Timmerman noted that Chicago has the research base and recently has begun turning it into real opportunity. The CQE also manages the Duality Accelerator, a startup incubator program that gives companies worldwide access to hard-to-come-by quantum infrastructure.
“In 2020 and 2021, we launched Duality as the first quantum-focused startup accelerator in the United States,” she said. “The portfolio spans quantum computing, communications, sensing, and enabling technologies. The enabling category is especially important because the quantum supply chain includes materials, components, subsystems, and full systems. As companies mature, they may move up that stack — from individual products to subsystems and, in some cases, complete systems. To date, Duality has supported roughly 25 to 30 startups. Some are homegrown. Some came to the region for the program and then moved here permanently. qBraid is one example. Others may not relocate entirely, but they keep an employee or office here because of the ecosystem. Still others return home after the program while maintaining research and talent connections in the region.”
The development of quantum infrastructure offers opportunities for semiconductor companies with roots in the region. “Quantum computing represents one of the most exciting long-term opportunities in advanced computing, and the Midwest’s growing research activity in this area is encouraging,” said Synopsys’ Salomone. “While quantum systems require fundamentally different architectures than conventional computing, they still rely on sophisticated design methodologies, simulation technologies, and increasingly complex semiconductor components. As quantum technologies mature, collaboration between hardware developers, research institutions, and technology providers will be essential. Synopsys sees opportunities to support the broader ecosystem through design, modeling, verification, and system development capabilities that help accelerate innovation and reduce development complexity. We believe the research leadership emerging from Midwestern institutions can contribute meaningfully to the future of quantum and hybrid computing technologies.”
Timmerman points to three broad opportunities for regional companies entering the quantum space:

For quantum technology developers: “Researchers at universities today may start companies tomorrow, and within two to five years those companies may be hiring significant numbers of people. That is the path from research to commercial opportunity in the region.”
For manufacturers: “We think about that in two ways — helping quantum developers move from bespoke research and development to scaled manufacturing, and making this region a destination where established manufacturers can join a domestic quantum supply chain that does not yet fully exist. We already have regional manufacturers producing materials such as diamond, as well as components such as vacuum systems and nanopositioners. There is an opportunity to help those companies scale and to reach additional manufacturers that may not yet understand quantum, the emerging supply chain, or where they could fit within it.”
For end users: “Quantum sensors are already at relatively high technology-readiness levels, and companies can buy and pilot systems today. Quantum networking and quantum computing are farther off. But this region should be among the fastest places to adopt quantum technologies because of the surrounding research and industry adjacencies. We were not necessarily at the forefront of early artificial-intelligence adoption, though that may be changing. With quantum, we have an opportunity to lead from the beginning.”

Startup support
Quantum startups are not the only new ventures getting institutional support in the Midwest. EDA companies, for example, have always provided tools and expertise to educational institutions, but in the past the goal was to hire new engineering graduates and relocate them back to existing tech hubs. What’s changed is that many new jobs are being created outside of those established hubs, where the cost of living is far lower than in places like Silicon Valley.
“Our role is to empower startups, universities, established manufacturers, and government-supported initiatives with the tools and expertise needed to accelerate innovation and strengthen the domestic semiconductor supply chain,” said Synopsys’ Salomone.
A major part of the MMEC’s work is helping regional entrepreneurs survive the so-called “Valley of Death” by giving members access to infrastructure capabilities, such as compute environments and design tools, at lower costs or through different cost models than has been available before. “Streamlining access to prototyping capabilities, whether that be tools to do epitaxial development, or the ability to do advanced packaging and module development and characterization and tests,” Casto said. “Even the access models that allow the demonstration of those in, say, relevant operational environments. We work closely with both the commercial and government sector, and even special labs and test ranges that will qualify and test those capabilities.”
This helps address one of the biggest needs for many startups in the Midwest — access to the tools that already exist in the region. “We are working with those companies in terms of developing intellectual property, which will make it easier for other companies to use the foundry ecosystems,” Casto said. “We’ve received a lot of feedback from those organizations and how they do their designs, and we’ve built those capabilities into our digital infrastructure at MMEC, so they can leverage those to be more competitive in the market. We can aggregate requirements and lower costs through economies of scale for other businesses to use. It really is a win-win environment as MMEC has scaled.”
